rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī takes Moses’ requested ḥukm as knowledge of God and His attributes; this knowledge, like being joined to the righteous, exists by God’s creation, not by favors already bestowed.
rows.anchor: لما ثبت أن المراد من الحكم العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The requested knowledge is neither distracting knowledge of other things nor basic knowledge required for faith, which Abraham already had; it is higher recognition of divine attributes, essence, or an inward unveiling beyond verbal description.
rows.anchor: فثبت أن المطلوب بهذا الدعاء درجات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī reads Abraham’s sequence as seeking knowledge first, then worldly perfections: inward virtue rather than outward appearance, and spiritual honor and lasting remembrance rather than wealth.
rows.anchor: ابتدأ بطلب ما هو الكمال الذاتي للإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He explains the wish for praise in two ways: gathered human attention may increase a person’s perfection, and public praise of virtue can inspire others to acquire the same virtues.
rows.anchor: إذا اجتمعت طائفة منها فربما قوي مجموعها على ما عجزت الآحاد عنه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says God granted Abraham this lasting good mention, as confirmed by the statement that his good name was left among later generations.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما وقد أعطاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation is that Abraham asks for a truthful caller to God among later generations, namely Muhammad; the phrase thus refers to Muhammad’s mission.
rows.anchor: من ذريته في آخر الزمان من يكون داعيا إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī presents the Quran’s eloquence as miraculous proof of prophethood, or its account of past events without prior instruction as proof that it came by revelation.
rows.anchor: لفصاحته معجز فيكون ذلك من رب العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier scriptures strengthen the proof: the seven prophetic narratives match their accounts without discrepancy, although Muhammad had not studied or prepared for them.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر هذه القصص السبع على ما هي موجودة في زبر الأولين من غير تفاوت أصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On either of the two readings of “the Spirit brought it down,” the preposition is causative: God caused the Spirit to descend bearing the revelation.
rows.anchor: ومعنى { نزل به الروح } جعل الله الروح نازلا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The faithful Spirit is Gabriel: he is called spirit because created from spirit, because he brings religious salvation like life, or because he is wholly spirit; he is trustworthy as revelation’s custodian.
rows.anchor: والروح الأمين جبريل عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made Gabriel bring the Quran to Muhammad’s heart, meaning He enabled him to understand and fixed it there so securely it would not be forgotten, as in 87:6.
rows.anchor: أي فهمك إياه وأثبته في قلبك

rows.speaker: النعمان بن بشير
rows.claim: Al-Nuʿmān b. Bashīr reports the Prophet’s saying that a sound heart makes the whole body sound, while a corrupt heart corrupts it.
rows.anchor: روى النعمان بن بشير قال سمعته عليه السلام يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī argues that the heart commands the limbs: awareness returns with the heart’s recovery, emotions alter the body, motives arise there, and it is the seat of reason.
rows.anchor: أن القلب منبع المشاق الباعثة على الأفعال الصادرة من سائر الأعضاء وإذا كانت المشاق مبادىء للأفعال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī favors the heart as the seat of reason: scripture places understanding and its opposites in the heart, introspection locates thought there, and it is central, first formed, and last to die.
rows.anchor: وكل ذلك يدل على أن موضع العقل هو القلب

rows.speaker: طائفة من القدماء
rows.claim: A group of earlier thinkers locate reason in the brain, rather than the heart.
rows.anchor: فإن طائفة من القدماء ذهبوا إلى أن معدن العقل هو الدماغ

rows.speaker: من قال العقل في الدماغ
rows.claim: The brain view cites the sensory and motor nerves’ connection to the brain, impaired reason after brain injury, common idiom, and the brain’s higher position.
rows.anchor: أن الحواس التي هي الآلات للإدراك نافذة إلى الدماغ دون القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī answers that sensory effects may pass through brain to heart and commands from heart through brain to limbs; brain health may mediate heart effects, idiom reflects temperature, and elevation would favor the skull, not brain.
rows.anchor: لم لا يجوز أن يقال الحواس تؤدي آثارها إلى الدماغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun may refer to the preceding reports, the Quran’s description, Muhammad’s description, or the warnings already discussed.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون المراد صفة القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You receive the Quran from a Wise, Knowing One” means it is given to Muhammad by an absolutely wise and knowing source; the indefinite adjectives stress this, and introduce Moses’ story.
rows.anchor: من عند أي حكيم وأي عليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening “when” is governed by an omitted imperative, “remember,” though it may instead depend on “Knowing.”
rows.anchor: منصوب بمضمر وهو اذكر كأنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling his wife “his family” implies that she alone accompanied Moses; this explains the later plural address, “stay here.”
rows.anchor: على أنه لم يكن مع موسى عليه السلام غير امرأته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They were traveling by night in cold weather and had lost the way; seeing a distant fire reassured them with hope of directions and warmth.
rows.anchor: المعنى أنهما كانا يسيران ليلا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One reported sense of “I perceived a fire” is that Moses saw or beheld it.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم المراد أبصرت ورأيت

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Another reported sense is that Moses came upon or found the fire and felt familiar with it.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون بل المراد صادفت ووجدت فآنست به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī prefers “saw,” since Arabic speakers do not distinguish “I perceived with my eye” from “I saw with my eye.”
rows.anchor: لأنهم لا يفرقون بين قول القائل آنست ببصري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With light hamza, “ ألا” is an attention particle followed by a vocative particle whose addressee is omitted; the cited verse illustrates the omission.
rows.anchor: للتنبيه ويا حرف النداء ومناداه محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With doubled lām, one parsing means Satan turned them from the path lest they prostrate, with a preposition omitted; alternatively “lā” is extra, meaning they are not guided except by prostrating.
rows.anchor: فحذف الجار مع أن ويجوز أن تكون لا مزيدة

rows.speaker: عبدالله، الأعمش
rows.claim: A reading attributed to ʿAbd Allāh and al-Aʿmash has “halla,” replacing the hamza with hāʾ.
rows.anchor: قراءة الأعمش هلا بقلب الهمزة هاء

rows.speaker: عبدالله
rows.claim: A further reading from ʿAbd Allāh addresses the audience directly: “Will you not prostrate?”
rows.anchor: وعن عبدالله هلا تسجدون بمعنى ألا تسجدون على الخطاب

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Abū’s reading has “Do they not prostrate to God?” and continues with God’s bringing forth hidden things and knowing what people conceal and disclose.
rows.anchor: قراءة أبي { إلا * يسجدون * لله الذى يخرج الخبء فى * السماوات

rows.speaker: أهل التحقيق
rows.claim: The investigators say the phrase must be a command: if it prohibited prostration, God’s power to reveal hidden things and knowledge of secrets would not support the wording.
rows.anchor: يجب أن يكون بمعنى الأمر لأنه لو كان بمعنى المنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The hidden thing” is a verbal noun used for what is hidden, encompassing provisions and wealth; God brings it from heaven through rain and from earth through plants.
rows.anchor: وهو يتناول جميع أنواع الأرزاق والأموال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse attributes both power to God, who brings hidden things forth, and knowledge, since He knows what people conceal and reveal.
rows.anchor: ويعلم ما تخفون وما تعلنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument refutes sun worship: deity requires universal power and knowledge, but the finite sun cannot be shown to bring hidden things forth or know secrets, nor therefore to secure benefits and avert harms.
rows.anchor: الشمس ليست كذلك فهي لا تكون إلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also reads heaven’s hidden thing as the sun emerging after its setting, under God’s control; earth’s hidden things include sperm from the loins and ribs and the embryo formed from it.
rows.anchor: هو الذي يخرج الشمس من المشرق بعد أفولها في المغرب فهذا هو إخراج الخبء في السموات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun’s setting and rising show it is governed by a sovereign, so worship belongs to its controller; the verse reverses Abraham’s and Moses’ order because this debate concerns sun worship.
rows.anchor: أفول الشمس وطلوعها يدلان على كونها تحت تدبير مدبر قاهر فكانت العبادة لقاهرها والمتصرف فيها أولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view treats “reached full strength” and “became settled” as synonymous: full strength, balanced temperament, and mature constitution.
rows.anchor: أحدهما : أنهما بمعنى واحد وهو استكمال القوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī calls it likelier that the terms differ: “full strength” is complete bodily power, while “settled” is complete intellectual power.
rows.anchor: وهو الأقرب أن الأشد عبارة عن كمال القوة الجسمانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second distinction makes “full strength” complete power and “settled” the completion of bodily constitution and form.
rows.anchor: الأشد عبارة عن كمال القوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third distinction takes “full strength” as reaching adulthood and “settled” as bodily perfection.
rows.anchor: الأشد عبارة عن البلوغ ، والاستواء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās places full strength from age 18 to 30, a plateau from 30 to 40, then decline; Rāzī endorses this trajectory and explains that bodily powers wane as intellect grows, making forty fitting for prophethood.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس الأشد ما بين الثمان عشرة سنة إلى الثلاثين ثم من الثلاثين سنة إلى الأربعين يبقى سواء

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the singular of “ashudd” would analogically be “shadd,” though that singular is unattested.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : الأشد واحدها شد في القياس

rows.speaker: أبو الهيثم
rows.claim: Abū al-Haytham gives “shidda” as the singular, paralleling “niʿma” as the singular of “anʿām”; shidda means strength and toughness.
rows.anchor: قال أبو الهيثم : واحد الأشد شدة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Moses did not set out for Midian but surrendered himself to God and walked without knowing where he was going until God brought him there.
rows.anchor: إنه خرج وما قصد مدين ولكنه سلم نفسه إلى الله تعالى وأخذ يمشي من غير معرفة

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others say Moses intended Midian because he thought its people were related to him through Midian son of Abraham, though he did not know the route and relied on God.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون لما خرج قصد مدين لأنه وقع في نفسه أن بينهم وبينه قرابة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view says Gabriel came and showed Moses the way to Midian.
rows.anchor: من الناس من قال بل جاءه جبريل عليه السلام

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī transmits from al-Suddī that an angel on horseback met Moses; Moses prostrated in joy, the angel stopped him, and Moses followed toward Midian.
rows.anchor: ذكر ابن جرير عن السدي لما أخذ موسى عليه السلام في المسير جاءه ملك على فرس فسجد له موسى من الفرح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī prefers that Moses meant to reach Midian but did not know the route: “toward Midian,” rather than “to Midian,” and his plea for guidance show uncertainty about the way, not the destination.
rows.anchor: والأقرب أن يقال إنه قصد الذهاب إلى مدين وما كان عالما بالطريق

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq says Moses left Egypt for Midian without provisions or a mount; the journey took eight days and he ate only leaves.
rows.anchor: قال ابن إسحاق خرج من مصر إلى مدين بغير زاد ولا ظهر

words: عسى ربى أن يهدينى سواء السبيل
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ plea resembles Abraham’s “I am going to my Lord; He will guide me”; Rāzī says Moses often echoes Abraham in argument, reply, prayer, and supplication.
rows.anchor: فهو نظير قول جده إبراهيم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The water was the source from which people watered, reportedly a well; “arrived at it” means reached it, “at it” means by its rim and watering place, and the group was numerous and diverse.
rows.anchor: ووروده مجيئه والوصول إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Below them” places the two women lower than the crowd; “tadhūdān” means to push away or hold back.
rows.anchor: الذود الدفع والطرد فقوله ( تذودان ) أي تحبسان

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says the women held their sheep back because stronger people at the water prevented them from watering.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج لأن على الماء من كان أقوى منهما فلا يتمكنان من السقي

rows.speaker: قول آخر
rows.claim: One explanation is that they held their sheep back because they disliked competing for water.
rows.anchor: كانتا تكرهان المزاحمة على الماء

rows.speaker: قول آخر
rows.claim: Another explanation is that they kept their flock separate from the other people’s animals.
rows.anchor: لئلا تختلط أغنامهما بأغنامهم

rows.speaker: قول آخر
rows.claim: Another explanation is that they avoided mixing with the men.
rows.anchor: لئلا تختلطا بالرجال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further reported interpretation is that they warded off onlookers so they would not look at their faces.
rows.anchor: كانتا تذودان عن وجوههما نظرا الناظر ليراهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that they kept people away from their flock.
rows.anchor: تذودان الناس عن غنمهما

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says they restrained the sheep so they would not scatter and wander off.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء تحبسانها عن أن تتفرق وتتسرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What is your business?” literally asks what matter or request they are pursuing by holding the flock back; “khatb” is used as “shaʾn” is in “what is your affair?”
rows.anchor: أي ما شأنكما وحقيقته ما مخطوبكما أي مطلوبكما من الذياد فسمى المخطوب خطبا

words: لا نسقى حتى يصدر الرعاء وأبونا شيخ كبير
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their answer shows weakness: women normally do not water, they had delayed their flock, awaited the herders’ departure and leftover water, and their elderly father could not come to do it.
rows.anchor: وذلك يدل على ضعفهما عن السقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses watered for them before the herders left, so the women returned to their father earlier than usual.
rows.anchor: فعند ذلك سقى لهما قبل صدر الرعاء

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو، ابن عامر، عاصم
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and ʿĀṣim read with fatḥa on yāʾ and ḍamma on dāl: the herders themselves depart from the water.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو وابن عامر وعاصم بفتح الياء

rows.speaker: الباقون
rows.claim: The remaining readers use ḍamma on yāʾ and kasra on dāl: the herders make their animals depart from the water.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الباقون بضم الياء ، وكسر الدال
